issues.legal_issue: A will cannot be accepted as genuine unless its propounder proves its due execution and, when suspicious circumstances attend its execution, satisfactorily removes those suspicions.
material_facts: The propounder prepared the draft and dictated the will to the scribe, and his sons received substantial benefits under it.

The will contained elaborate recitals supporting the testatrix’s title and capacity to dispose of the properties, some of which were inconsistent with the evidence or had not been accepted by the courts below.
The evidence did not satisfactorily establish that the testatrix had approved the draft or understood the will’s contents and dispositions before signing it.
The testatrix’s signatures were proved, but the attesting evidence was inconclusive or inconsistent on whether the will had been read to her and understood by her.
The testatrix was ill and unable to leave her bed, although unconsciousness was not proved.
issues.conclusion: The propounder did not discharge the burden of proving the will in the face of the suspicious circumstances, and the High Court was right to find that due and valid execution had not been established.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, the propounder must prove the testator’s signature, testamentary capacity, understanding and approval of the dispositions, and execution with the required attestation. Proof is assessed by the satisfaction of a prudent mind, not mathematical certainty. Where suspicious circumstances arise, the initial burden becomes heavier and the propounder must remove legitimate suspicions by cogent and satisfactory evidence; a prominent role in execution coupled with substantial benefit is itself generally suspicious. The Court applied Barry v. Butlin, Fulton v. Andrew, Vellasawmy Servai v. Sivaraman Servai, Sarat Kumari Bibi v. Sakhi Chand, and Harmes v. Hinkson. Allegations of fraud, coercion, or undue influence must be proved by the person making them, but circumstances independently raising doubt must be addressed by the propounder.

rule.if: will_validity_proceeding and will_propounded and suspicious_execution_circumstances and propounder_took_prominent_role and propounders_close_beneficiaries_received_substantial_benefit and not satisfactory_explanation_of_suspicion

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a document propounded as a will is the testator’s valid will.
predicates.will_propounded: A person relies on the document as the testator’s will and seeks to establish it.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances of preparation or execution, or the document’s contents and dispositions, give the court legitimate reason to doubt that the document expresses the testator’s free and informed intentions.
predicates.propounder_took_prominent_role: The person relying on the will took a prominent part in preparing or procuring its execution.
predicates.propounders_close_beneficiaries_received: People closely connected to the propounder received substantial benefits under the will.
predicates.satisfactory_explanation_of_suspicion: The propounder presented cogent and satisfactory evidence that removed the legitimate doubts about the will’s execution and the testator’s understanding and approval.

issues.definition: When a will is propounded in a will-validity proceeding, suspicious circumstances remain unexplained, and the propounder took a prominent role while closely connected beneficiaries received substantial benefits, the will is not accepted as genuine.

issues.legal_issue: Proof of a testator’s signature does not by itself establish the testator’s knowledge and approval of the contents of a will when suspicious circumstances call that approval into doubt.
material_facts: The testatrix’s signatures at five places on the will were proved.
The trial court treated proof of the signatures as raising a presumption that the testatrix knew the contents of the will.
The evidence did not satisfactorily show that the will was fully read to the testatrix or that she understood and approved its contents.
The circumstances surrounding preparation and execution of the will were suspicious.
issues.conclusion: The trial court erred in treating proof of the testatrix’s signatures as a presumption that she knew the contents of the will; the signatures did not resolve the doubts about her understanding and approval.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, govern proof of signature and execution of an attested will, but proof of a signature alone does not establish knowledge and approval where suspicious circumstances remain. The Court explained and approved Surendra Nath Chatterji v. Jahnavi Charan Mukherji to the extent that any presumption from signature is liable to be rebutted by proof of suspicious circumstances.

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether a document propounded as a will is the testator’s valid will.
predicates.testator_signature_proved: Evidence establishes that the testator signed or marked the document.
predicates.suspicious_execution_circumstances: The circumstances of preparation or execution, or the document’s contents and dispositions, give the court legitimate reason to doubt that the document expresses the testator’s free and informed intentions.

issues.definition: When a testator’s signature is proved in a will-validity proceeding but suspicious execution circumstances exist, the signature alone does not establish knowledge and approval of the will’s contents.

issues.legal_issue: Findings on other property-title issues should not be treated as decided when the reviewing court finds that the will on which the claim depended was not proved and the other issues were not properly considered.
material_facts: The High Court rejected the will but also expressed conclusions about the source of funds for certain property acquisitions and whether the testatrix retained an interest in the properties.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not fully or properly considered the evidence relevant to those property issues.
The Supreme Court concluded that the property issues need not be decided to dispose of the appeal concerning the will.
issues.conclusion: The property-title issues were not decided in the appeal and could be considered afresh if they arose between the parties.
issues.legal_principle: A court should not decide collateral issues unnecessarily after resolving the principal issue, particularly where the relevant evidence has not been fully or properly considered; conclusions expressed on those issues in those circumstances do not determine them for later consideration.

rule.if: appeal_involving_will_validity and will_not_proved and lower_court_also_decided_collateral_property_issues and collateral_evidence_not_fully_considered

predicates.appeal_involving_will_validity: The proceeding is an appeal in which a claim depends on establishing a will.
predicates.will_not_proved: The court finds that the propounder has not proved the will.
predicates.lower_court_also_decided_collateral_prop: The lower court expressed conclusions on property issues beyond the validity of the will.
predicates.collateral_evidence_not_fully_considered: The evidence relevant to those collateral property issues was not fully or properly considered.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a will, the will is not proved, and the lower court decided collateral property issues without fully considering their evidence, those property issues remain open.
